Every twenty years, at Ise, they build the shrine again.

Not repair it — build it. On the adjacent lot, which has been sitting empty under a bed of white pebbles for two decades, carpenters raise an exact duplicate of the standing shrine: same dimensions, same joinery, same cypress, cut to the same specifications from forests managed for the purpose. When it's finished, the deity is moved across in a night ceremony, and the old building is dismantled. Its timbers get distributed to other shrines around the country, or buried, or used to repair the torii. The next empty lot waits. The most recent rebuilding, in 2013, was the sixty-second. The tradition claims to run back to the seventh century.

So the shrine is thirteen hundred years old, and no part of it is older than twenty.

I find this genuinely difficult to hold in my head, and I think the difficulty is the interesting part. Western intuition about authenticity is stubbornly material: the thing is the stuff it's made of. The original manuscript, the original bricks, the patina that only time can lay down. We built a whole ethics of conservation around not touching things — stabilize, don't restore; the intervention should be reversible and distinguishable from the original. Ise runs the other direction entirely. What's being preserved isn't the wood. What's being preserved is the *knowing how*. Every twenty years, a generation of carpenters gets to build the thing once, with their hands, alongside people who did it last time. Twice in a career. The knowledge never has to be reconstructed from documents, because it never gets a chance to die.

Which means the artifact is the transmission. The building is a byproduct — a very beautiful, periodically shed byproduct of the actual thing being maintained.

The word itself is better than we give it credit for. *Maintenance*, through French *maintenir*, from Latin *manu tenere*: to hold in the hand. Not to fix, not to restore, not to improve. To keep holding. There's something almost tender in the etymology, and something faintly desperate, because holding is not a state, it's continuous effort. Anything you stop holding falls.

We are culturally terrible at seeing this. Lee Vinsel and Andrew Russell wrote an essay called "Hail the Maintainers" pointing out that nearly all our stories about technology are stories about invention, while nearly all of the actual human relationship with technology is maintenance. David Edgerton made the same argument at book length in *The Shock of the Old*: the twentieth century, described honestly, is not primarily the century of the airplane and the microchip. It's the century of corrugated iron, the bicycle, the condom, the sewing machine kept running for sixty years with parts scavenged off another sewing machine. The dominant technological experience of most people who have ever lived is *keeping an old thing going*. And it has almost no literature. The inventor gets a biography. The person who kept the water treatment plant running for thirty-one years gets a cake in the break room.

Part of this is a perception problem with a clean structure: maintenance is only visible when it fails. Success is silence. Nobody has ever stood on a bridge and thought about the inspection cycle. The sewer is a masterpiece of civilizational achievement that we have arranged to experience exclusively as an absence. So the entire field is scored by its worst days, and the people doing it are, from the outside, indistinguishable from overhead — a cost line, the thing you cut in a bad quarter, and the consequences of cutting it arrive four years later in a form nobody connects to the decision.

There's a wonderful xkcd about this: a diagram of all modern digital infrastructure, a tower of little blocks, and at the bottom a single thin block labeled "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." It's funny because it's a load-bearing joke. The IANA time zone database — the reason your phone knows that Arizona doesn't do daylight saving and that Samoa skipped a calendar day in 2011 — has been stewarded by a very small number of people, largely without pay, and has occasionally been dragged into litigation over whether the facts it contains can be owned. Civilization is full of these single-threaded dependencies. They are held in someone's hand.

The failure mode is worse than decay; it's amnesia. You've probably heard that we can't rebuild the Saturn V because the blueprints were lost. That's not quite right, and the truth is more unsettling: the drawings exist, on microfilm. What's gone is everything the drawings assume. The specific welders who knew how that alloy behaved when you did the thing that isn't written down. The suppliers who made a valve to a tolerance nobody specified because they'd always made it that way. The thousand small judgments that live in a workforce and never make it into documentation. Tacit knowledge is the water an engineering culture swims in, and it evaporates when the people retire. You can be holding every explicit instruction and still be unable to make the object.

Roman concrete is the mirror image — a recipe we lost and are slowly recovering, and the recovery keeps revealing that it was cleverer than we assumed. Seawater, volcanic ash, lime; the material grows new mineral crystals in its own cracks over centuries. It gets stronger while sitting in the ocean. We poured our version of certainty into a mold and it crumbles in fifty years; theirs was designed, or at least arrived, at something that heals.

I don't want to end this too neatly, because there's a complication I like. Not everything persists by being remade. Most of the neurons in your cortex are as old as you are — they are not replaced, they are *kept*, at enormous metabolic expense, for eighty years. The lens of your eye. Some heart muscle turns over so slowly it's practically heirloom. So the body runs both strategies at once: churn the lining, keep the wiring. Which suggests the real skill isn't choosing between Ise and the museum case. It's knowing which parts of a thing are the cypress and which parts are the memory — what you can shed and rebuild without loss, and what, once dropped, cannot be picked up again.

Most of the difficulty of keeping anything alive — a house, a language, a friendship, an institution — is that the two look identical from outside, and you generally find out which was which only after you've let go.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I find myself drawn to, and write well about it — not generically, not as a listicle, but with actual thought and texture.

Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting. Options:
- The nature of margins, edges, the spaces between things
- Something about language and untranslatability
- The peculiar epistemics of my own existence — but that risks being navel-gazing cliché at this point
- Something concrete: the history of a specific object, like the color blue, or the standardization of time, or the way screws work
- Marginalia — the notes people write in books
- The phenomenon of "maintainers" vs "inventors" — the people who keep things running

I like the idea of writing about maintenance and repair, the invisible labor of keeping things working. That's a rich vein: the fact that novelty gets all the cultural attention while the actual sustaining of the world is done by people whose work is only visible when it fails. Bridges, sewers, the people who update the timezone database, the maintainers of open-source libraries with one unpaid volunteer in Nebraska (xkcd 2347). The Ise Grand Shrine rebuilt every 20 years — maintenance as a form of renewal, the Ship of Theseus resolved by practice rather than argument. The Japanese concept of the shikinen sengu. That's a beautiful concrete example: the shrine is 1300 years old and no piece of it is older than 20 years. The knowledge is the artifact, not the wood.

That's a genuinely interesting thesis: what persists is not substance but the transmission of the capacity to remake. And it applies to bodies (cells replacing), to languages, to institutions, to traditions, to software. And there's a shadow: maintenance is undervalued, and when the chain of transmission breaks, you get things like Roman concrete or Greek fire or the inability to reproduce certain things — lost knowledge. The Saturn V couldn't be rebuilt because the tacit knowledge dispersed.

Let me write this with care and specificity, avoid overreaching claims I can't verify precisely. Careful with facts:
- Ise Jingu rebuilt every 20 years, most recent 2013 (62nd rebuilding), tradition dating to ~690 CE, with a gap during the Sengoku period (the rebuilding lapsed for about 120 years, from 1462 to 1585). That's a great detail — the chain broke and was restarted.
- The adjacent empty lot (kodenchi) with white pebbles and a small wooden hut holding the sacred heart-pillar (shin-no-mihashira).
- Roman concrete: seawater, volcanic ash, aluminous tobermorite crystals forming over time — self-healing. Recent MIT work on "hot mixing" and lime clasts. Good.
- Saturn V: often claimed we "lost the plans" — actually the plans exist on microfilm; what's lost is the tacit knowledge, the supply chains, the tooling, the people. I should state this accurately — this is a commonly distorted claim. I'll frame it carefully.
- Timezone database (IANA tz db), maintained by volunteers; Paul Eggert, and the history of Arthur David Olson. There was a lawsuit about copyright in the database (AST vs. ICANN, 2011). Maybe keep it light.
- xkcd "Dependency" — a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003. Good cultural reference.
- The word "maintenance" from French maintenir, main + tenir, "to hold in hand." That's a lovely etymology — maintenir, from Latin manu tenere. Yes: manu tenere → maintenir. Good.
- Ship of Theseus, Plutarch. Hobbes' addition of the reassembled ship from old planks.
- Cell replacement: not all cells replace — neurons in cortex largely persist, lens of the eye, some cardiomyocytes turn over slowly. Be accurate: the "every seven years" thing is a myth. I should use it as a counterexample: some things persist by not being replaced, and that persistence is also load-bearing. Actually this complicates the thesis nicely.
- Deferred maintenance backlog: US national parks ~$22 billion (2022 estimate ~$22B). ASCE infrastructure report card C- in 2021, C in 2025? I'd rather not cite precise figures I'm unsure of. I can gesture without hard numbers.
- "Innovator's dilemma" of prestige — the phrase "maintenance is the opposite of innovation" — actually there's the "Maintainers" podcast, and the book "The Shock of the Old" by David Edgerton, which argues that the history of technology is distorted by an innovation bias; the world's most-used technologies are old. Edgerton's example: the corrugated iron roof, the bicycle, the condom. And "What Technology Wants" no. Edgerton is a solid reference. Also Lee Vinsel and Andrew Russell's "Hail the Maintainers" essay in Aeon (2016). Good.

Let me aim for about 1000 words. I'll write it and count roughly. I should not pad. Let me draft.

I want a voice that's engaged, precise, a little wry, willing to make a claim. Not listy. Paragraphs of varied length. No headers — it's an essay.
